read: full: main text pp. 1-10 and appendices A-C.5 (pp. 14-22) read in full; C.6 and D-H (physics-metric details, agent implementation, qualitative analysis, SWE-agent, prompts; pp. 22-39) skimmed
venue_now: Preprint, under review (p. 1 header); the text is arXiv v1, 8 Apr 2025 (p. 1). papers.json notes only NeurIPS 2024 workshop versions, no archival venue
what_it_is: FEABench tests whether LLMs and LLM agents can solve physics, mathematics and engineering problems by operating the finite element software COMSOL Multiphysics through its Java API (pp. 1-3). FEABench Gold holds 15 manually verified problems derived from COMSOL Application Gallery tutorials, each with model specifications, a step-by-step plan, a target value, ground-truth API code and a model tree. FEABench Large holds 200 algorithmically parsed tutorial tasks without a verifiable target (pp. 2-3). Models write API calls from either the specification (ModelSpecs task) or the plan (Plan task) (p. 3). Evaluation combines execution-based and intermediate metrics: executability, model-tree similarity to the ground-truth model, physics interface and feature recall, an LLM-checked valid target, and relative error within 10% (pp. 5-6). Six LLMs were tested at baseline. A multi-turn agent with tools and execution feedback reaches 0.88 executability, but valid targets for at most 2 of 15 problems in COMSOL (pp. 6-9).
domain: engineering and physics simulation: multiphysics finite element analysis in COMSOL (e.g. heat transfer, eigenfrequency analysis of a beam and a quantum dot, also a Black-Scholes option model) (p. 3)
size: FEABench Gold 15 problems; FEABench Large 200 tasks; a 768-snippet annotated code library used only for retrieval (pp. 2-3); 6 LLMs on Gold and 3 closed models on Large (pp. 6-7)
source_of_items: COMSOL Application Gallery tutorials. The first 2-3 Gold problems were annotated by hand by an expert COMSOL user; the rest have LLM-drafted specifications and plans that humans edited and verified (pp. 3, 14-15). Large is parsed algorithmically (pp. 3, 19).
has_gold_traces: partial: each Gold problem has a step-by-step Plan of modelling instructions, executable ground-truth API code and a model tree, which the paper calls 'a high-level lossy representation of a solution path' (p. 3). There is no gold chain of intermediate numerical results
evaluation: Multi-metric, beyond the final answer (pp. 5-6, 20-22). Executability: the fraction of API lines that run. Model Tree Score: similarity of the built model tree to the ground-truth tree, which 'measures the alignment of the model's solution path with a successful path'. Physics metrics: interface factuality, interface/feature/property recall against the ground-truth code, feature dimension. Valid Target: an LLM (Gemini-1.5-Pro) judges whether the exported value is the target quantity. Relative Error | Strict: a valid target within 10%. Code similarity (difflib) is reported only as a baseline (p. 19). No step-level check of reasoning
human_validation: Gold problems were manually confirmed to be self-sufficient and solvable, and the ground-truth code was run to confirm that it exports the target (pp. 2, 15). No human validation of the metrics or of the LLM Valid-Target check is reported.
contamination_measures: none; the tutorials and models are publicly available on the COMSOL website (p. 10)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-E2 (L190-193): 'Others focus on tangential skills such as design generation (Guo et al., 2025b) or software proficiency (Mudur et al., 2025)'. S-I3c (L116-122): 'unlike existing benchmarks (e.g., Zhou et al., 2025; Mudur et al., 2025) that rely solely on outcome matching, demand holistic procedural reasoning'. The closing generalisation S-E3 (L199-201): 'existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching'.
engtrace_use.explanation: S-I3c, and S-E3 as it applies here, contradict the paper. FEABench says pass@k-style outcome metrics are hard to apply because most solutions never compute a target (p. 5). It introduces 'a holistic automated evaluation strategy with intermediate metrics that seek to measure different facets of distance to a correct solution' (p. 2). Its Model Tree Score 'measures the alignment of the model's solution path with a successful path', and its physics metrics 'offer a granular look into the LLM's physics reasoning path' (p. 6). These intermediate metrics are what the paper reports (Tables 2-6, pp. 7-9). The outcome metric is never averaged, because only one problem passed it, and that one only by exporting a default value (p. 9). So I rate the use wrong rather than misleading: intermediate scoring is FEABench's main evaluation, not an add-on to outcome scoring. S-E2 on its own is imprecise. Operating COMSOL through its API is central, and the authors find that translating decisions into code is the larger bottleneck (p. 8). But the benchmark also requires spatial and physics decisions such as boundary conditions (p. 2), its title targets multiphysics reasoning, and FEA is core engineering practice (p. 1), so 'tangential' and 'software proficiency' undersell it.

suggested_wording: FEABench (Mudur et al., 2025) has models solve 15 manually verified multiphysics problems by writing COMSOL Multiphysics API calls, and scores partial progress by code executability, by the similarity of the built model to a ground-truth model and by recall of physics features, as well as by the computed target value; its ground truth is executable code, not a reasoning trace.
facts_to_cite: FEABench Gold: 15 manually verified problems derived from COMSOL Application Gallery tutorials; FEABench Large: 200 algorithmically parsed tutorial tasks without a verifiable numerical target (pp. 2-3)
The model must turn a natural-language problem description (ModelSpecs) or a step-by-step plan (Plan) into Java API calls that build the finite element model and export a target value (pp. 2-4)
Each Gold problem includes model specifications, a plan, a target value, ground-truth API code and a model tree (p. 3)

Metrics: executability, Model Tree Score, physics metrics (interface factuality, interface/feature/property recall, feature dimension), Valid Target (LLM-checked) and Relative Error | Strict (within 10%) (pp. 5-6, 21-22)
Baseline LLMs: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro and three Gemma-family models; the closed models reach executability of about 0.60-0.79 (pp. 6-7)
A multi-turn agent with API feedback, a verifier LLM and retrieval tools raises executability from 0.62 to 0.88, but produces valid targets for only 2 of 15 problems (Table 5, p. 9)
Only one problem passed the strict cut, and only by exporting a default temperature, so mean relative error is not reported (p. 9)
Translating decisions into valid API calls is a larger bottleneck than making the modelling decisions (p. 8)
With SWE-agent in Python, 11 problems yield a valid target and 4 pass the strict cut (p. 9)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: physics-based engineering subject matter (heat transfer and structural problems, close to EngTrace's mechanical and chemical transport domains); gold solution artefacts; metrics beyond the final answer that compare the solution path with a ground truth. Lacks: generated instances (15 static problems from public tutorials); contamination measures; checks of intermediate numerical reasoning (its intermediate metrics compare code and model-tree structure, not computed quantities); expert validation of any metric (Valid Target rests on an unvalidated LLM check); scale. Differs in task: it needs tool use and a COMSOL licence (p. 10), while EngTrace scores closed-book reasoning traces.
notes: EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025, p. 3) itself groups FEABench with 'task-oriented' evaluations, i.e. scored by executable outputs, so pairing the two as outcome-only examples in S-I3c is wrong for both, in different ways. The May reference (arXiv:2504.06260) matches this text (v1). The revised text should credit FEABench for scoring partial progress against a ground-truth solution path, and say what EngTrace does differently: it checks the computed intermediate quantities of a reasoning trace. On the verdict label: the protocol's misleading example (an outcome-only label on a benchmark that also scores steps) does not quite fit, because FEABench's intermediate metrics are its primary reported measures.
